newsitem.title: USA: Cash spill becomes "morality play" in Miami.
newsitem.headline: Cash spill becomes "morality play" in Miami.

text.p: Miami police examined videotapes on Monday in a search for lawbreakers who picked up cash, coins and food stamps from a wrecked armoured car as educators turned the incident into a lesson in right and wrong.

A 48-hour amnesty that allowed thieves to return portions of an estimated $550,000 in missing money ended on Saturday with just two people, a mother of six and an 11-year-old boy, voluntarily giving up their parts of the loot.

But some educators in Miami's inner city -- where last week residents called the Brink's accident "Christmas in January" and "Pennies from Heaven" -- hailed the incident as a golden opportunity to teach children right from wrong.
"It's a morality play that's playing itself out in Overtown," said Jack Lau, a pastor at St. Francis Xavier, a private school and church in the area where the truck crashed.
Dozens of people called Miami police over the weekend from as far away as California and Alaska, offering money to the woman and the boy as rewards for their honesty.
Police said their next step was to begin an active search for people, many of whom scrambled on hands and knees in broad daylight before TV cameras to pocket the dough.
"We're looking at videotapes of people picking up money. We've brought in people from the community to help us identify them," Lt. Bill Schwartz, a Miami police spokesman, said.

The Brink's truck, carrying as much as $3.7 million in cash and food stamps, overturned on Wednesday on a highway overpass, spilling some of its cargo into a street in Overtown, one of Miami's poorest neighbourhoods.
Dozens of passersby loaded coins into pockets, hats and shopping bags, calling the loot "pennies from heaven."
The truck also disgorged bags of bundled currency. A firefighter at the scene retrieved a sack containing more than $300,000 and a similar bag was found, slashed and emptied.

Herbert Tarvin, the boy who turned over to his teacher 85 cents he had picked up, took the money to police headquarters on Monday. On Friday, Faye McFadden, 40, returned $19.53 in quarters and pennies that she had gathered in a shopping bag.
"Her kids saw her on TV picking up coins," Schwartz said. "They were so ashamed of her and she couldn't explain why she was doing it, so she turned it (the money) in."
The theft of the Brink's horde has stirred vigorous debate in the local media -- some defending poor inner-city residents who scooped up cash and others criticising their dishonesty.
At Tarvin's school, St. Francis Xavier, in the heart of Overtown, teachers lauded their pupil and seized the opportunity as a lesson for students in morality.

"It's an education for everybody in the community. If you do right, it pays," Lau said. "What has made this an issue is that people are looking for hope and honesty. They are looking to a child to tell them what's true."
Police said they would likely arrest only those who had stolen large amounts of cash and food stamps.
"I'm not going to go over and grab some little old lady who grabbed a handful of quarters," Schwartz said.
Police had made two arrests by Monday, charging two women, one a Dade County corrections employee, for allegedly trying to use food stamps from the truck crash site.
